summary: Hikers find it very fast and convenient when new, with a wide mouth that makes scooping and drinking easy. The main complaint is clogging: flow often drops sharply after a few trips or after storage, especially in silty water, and cleaning only sometimes restores it. The soft flasks also develop pinhole leaks. Better suited to short trips with clear water than long thru-hikes.

Hikers find it very roomy for two and often a palace for one, light for its size, and solid in wind and rain once pitched properly. The main downside is a large footprint that is hard to fit into crowded or uneven sites, plus a learning curve to get a taut pitch. Some report condensation. Too big for a few solo hikers, though many enjoy the extra space.

Hikers praise it for generous vestibules, headroom and storm performance, and for being simple to pitch once the technique is learned. The most common drawback is a big footprint that gives a fairly snug sleeping area, which some bigger or taller hikers find cramped, though others of similar height are happy. Suits solo hikers who value weather protection and gear space.

Light and versatile, and many hikers sleep warm in it, but nearly as many find it colder than its rating. Drafts when rolling over and down shifting or cold spots come up often, and comfort limits are frequently reported well above the rated temperature. Works best with pad straps, a draft collar and layers, and best for people who sleep warm.

Many hikers find it light and comfortable, with roomy, well-placed pockets and a good price for the weight. Complaints fall into two groups: comfort problems such as a slipping hip belt, shoulder pain and back sweat, especially with heavier loads, and thin fabric that tears or frays. Best for moderate loads on established trails.

Comfortable for most hikers, carrying heavy loads well while staying light, roomy and good value. Some find it does not fit them, with hip belt, shoulder or frame issues, and a sweaty back comes up often. Water resistance is a plus for several.

Hikers find it very durable and comfortable at moderate loads, with an adjustable hip belt, plenty of room and a good fit for a bear canister. Comfort fades once loads climb past roughly 30 to 35 lb, and a few report a sweaty back or poor fit on thin frames. Not the lightest, and can be more pack than a small kit needs. Customer service is praised.

Hikers describe it as long-lived and trusted by many, often paired with a CNOC bag for gravity filtering, and easy to backflush. The main complaint is slowing or clogging, especially after storage or in silty water, which some revive with soaking and backflushing and others never fully fix. Squeezing bags by hand gets tedious on long trips.

Hikers say it is fuel efficient, light, quick to boil and strong in wind, with good flame control. The main weak spot is the piezo igniter, which can fail or stop working when wet, so many carry a backup lighter. It is also bulky to nest in small pots with a canister, and some find the pot stand fussy.

Hikers say it is roomy, light, packs small and is easy to pitch for many once the technique is learned, with good value. The main complaint is condensation, with damp heads and footboxes where the walls sag, especially for taller sleepers. The pitch has to be exact to avoid sagging, and some find it too short or confining.

Hikers find it comfortable for most, with a light frame that moves weight to the hips and a surprisingly roomy interior for its size. Fit varies, and some find it uncomfortable at heavier loads or too small in the pockets for bottles. A few report durability problems such as the frame poking through the base or hip belt tearing, several on early versions.

Light and packable, and warm for many hikers, who take it near or below the rating with layers. A sizable group find it colder than rated, with drafts and down shifting in the long baffles. Ratings read more like limits than comfort figures, so it suits those who sleep warm or choose a warmer version.

Hikers say fast flow, easy to backflush with a bottle, a field integrity check and caps on both ends make it a favorite for many, often preferred over a Sawyer. Quality control is the main worry: some units arrive duds, fail the integrity test or have poor flow, and a few clog on silty water and never recover.

Hikers say it is very light, compact and comfortable, and quieter than the XLite. The main complaint is fragility, with punctures, slow leaks and baffle or valve failures, sometimes within weeks. Many use a thin foam pad underneath and carry a repair kit. Also not very warm near freezing for some.

Hikers find it tough and water resistant, and comfortable for many at moderate loads. The main complaint is shoulder pain with heavier loads, thin straps and no load lifters, with several reaching their limit around 25 to 30 lb. Price and hard-to-reach bottle pockets also come up. Best for lighter kits.

Hikers find it light, roomy and storm-worthy, with a quick pitch once learned. Downsides are a big footprint that is hard to place on uneven or tight sites, some condensation, and a floor some find delicate. A few find it tight for two or for tall sleepers, who often lie diagonally.

Very comfortable, especially for side sleepers thanks to raised rails, and warm enough for many in cool weather. A good number find it colder than its rating near or below freezing, and some report leaks, loose insulation or weld pinholes. It is on the heavy side and a few find it noisy.

Hikers find it roomy, freestanding and solid in wind and rain, and quick to pitch for most. It is not the lightest for a solo tent. A few report durability problems with poles, inner mesh or floor, and some find the single-door layout or the shape fiddly or confining.

Comfortable, especially for side sleepers, and warm enough for cold nights, while staying light and packing small. Downsides are scattered: some still feel cold or find it balloon-like, a few find it noisy, and a few report leaks.

Hikers say it is compact, sturdy and good value, with stable pot supports, good wind resistance and a solid simmer. The weak spot is the built-in piezo igniter, which a few say failed. Some find it loud.

Most hikers find the Zpacks Arc Haul Ultra very comfortable and well ventilated for how light it is, even with heavy loads, and many say it has held up over long distances. The main downside is durability problems for some, such as worn stays, tears and stitching, and it gets expensive once add-ons are included.

Most hikers describe the ULA Ohm 2.0 as a durable, comfortable framed pack that carries multi-day loads well, with roomy side pockets, and the frame and belt can be removed to save weight. It is heavier than true ultralight packs, and a few found the shape, small back pocket or bear can fit awkward.

Most hikers find the Katabatic Gear Flex 30°F Quilt warm for its rating, often comfortable around freezing and below, and well made, with a pad attachment system many call the best around. It needs a warm enough pad, and for summer-only use a few found it more than they needed.

Most hikers like the Tarptent Notch as a light, roomy, weatherproof one-person tent that holds up well over many nights and handles wind. The main downsides are condensation or rain splash in heavy rain, a pitch that can be fiddly at first, and an inner that some taller people find coffin-like.

Most hikers rate the Durston X-Mid 2 Solid as a roomy, weatherproof shelter that copes well with storms, wind and cold, and many have used it for dozens of nights. Downsides include a large footprint and tricky pitching on uneven ground, discomfort in warm humid weather, and a few reports of floor or fabric damage.

Most hikers like the Tarptent Notch Li as a light, fast-pitching, storm-worthy solo tent that has held up on thru-hikes. Condensation is the most common complaint, mostly when poles are set low, though many report none. The interior is narrow and small for bigger or taller people, and the struts limit how it packs.

Most hikers find the Western Mountaineering UltraLite very warm for its weight and well made, with many using it into the 20s or teens and some for many years. A few cold sleepers found it did not match the hype, and the snug cut, shallow hood and packed size bothered some.

Most hikers like the Durston X-Mid Pro 2+ for its generous space for two people, a dog and gear, at a low weight, and it gets easier to pitch with practice. The big footprint needs a large flat site, condensation shows up on cold moist nights, and a few had floor or pole damage.

Most hikers find the Gossamer Gear G4-20 Ultralight 42 a comfortable, roomy and light frameless pack, best while loads stay in the low to mid 20s of pounds. Comfort drops with heavier loads, and some report torn mesh or stitching, fragile buckles, a sweaty back, or thinner padding on the newer version.

Most hikers find the NEMO Tensor Elite surprisingly comfortable, especially side sleepers, and it packs down very small and light. Common downsides are a slippery surface and poor insulation in cool weather, and it punctures more easily than heavier pads, so many pair it with a thin foam pad underneath.

Most hikers like the Tarptent Aeon Li as a very light, easy-pitching solo tent with a small footprint that does well in wind and has covered long trails. The downsides are a snug interior for taller hikers, condensation typical of single-wall tents, and struts that make it long and awkward to pack.

Most hikers value the Therm-a-Rest Z Lite SOL as a simple, tough foam pad that cannot be punctured and is warm enough for many conditions. The main downside is comfort: it is firm, side sleepers often get sore hips, and it compresses with use. A few found condensation pooling in the dimples.

Most hikers find the ULA Catalyst a very comfortable, durable pack for heavy loads, with room for a bear canister and long food carries, and some have taken it thousands of miles. Its size is more than needed for lighter solo trips, a few found it uncomfortable well past about 40 lb, and some saw tears or hip belt problems.

Most hikers praise the Mountain Laurel Designs DuoMid as a stormworthy pyramid shelter that handles wind, rain and snow, with plenty of room for one person, gear and often a dog. A couple of hikers had trouble with wet walls from condensation when pitched low, and it is floorless, so some add an inner.

Most hikers like the Platypus GravityWorks for groups and camp use: it filters a lot of water quickly while hanging, and many have used one for years. The main downside is clogging or slow flow, often after storage, and it is heavier and fussier than squeeze filters, so some use it only for groups.

Most hikers find the Gossamer Gear Gorilla 50 very comfortable and a good value for a light pack. Complaints centre on the hip belt, which some could not get to fit, and on durability, with a few reports of stitching ripping or holes. The main body is smaller than the name suggests, which strains with a bear canister or lots of food.

Most hikers use the Gossamer Gear Thinlight Foam Pad as a light add-on under an inflatable pad, where it protects against punctures, stops sliding and works as a sit pad. As a standalone bed it is too thin for some, and toughness is mixed, with a few reporting it tearing in brush or at folds.

Most hikers, many of them cold sleepers, find the Katabatic Gear Sawatch 15°F Quilt genuinely warm and well made, with a pad attachment system and cut that limit drafts. It can be too warm for summer, and one hiker found the wide size a bit too wide.

Hikers are split on the Sawyer Micro Squeeze. Some find it a light, decent filter for shorter trips or day kits that still works after storage, but many report flow that slows quickly or clogs, and say the regular Squeeze is faster and worth the extra weight. A few had it crack or come apart.

Most hikers find the Western Mountaineering VersaLite very warm and well made, and cold sleepers especially love it, with some bags lasting many years. It is more bag than some need, and a few found it overkill, bulky or too warm for three-season trips.

Most hikers like the Tarptent ProTrail Li as a roomy, small-packing solo tent, with enough length and clearance for tall people and thick pads. Condensation is the most common complaint, and the pitch can be finicky, with a couple of hikers distrusting it in strong wind.

Most hikers like the Durston X-Mid Pro 1 for its roomy interior and headroom, solid weather performance with a low pitch and zippered doors, and tough build. The main downsides are a fussy pitch on uneven ground and condensation as a single-wall tent. A few find it too narrow or too big.

Most hikers love the Tarptent Double Rainbow Li for its generous room, light weight, easy pitch and good wind stability, and it suits tall hikers well. Condensation is the main complaint, though several report very little. Two people fit but it gets tight, and a few had carbon pole damage.

Most hikers find the Big Agnes Tiger Wall UL2 light, very roomy for one and easy to pitch, with many logging long thru-hikes without trouble. Downsides are snagging zippers, delicate fabric that can tear or wear through, and some leaking in prolonged rain. It is semi-freestanding and snug for two.

Most hikers prize the Six Moon Designs Gatewood Cape as a very light, compact shelter that doubles as a poncho, and many have used it for years. Condensation and limited wind performance are the main drawbacks, and it is small for anyone around six feet or taller. It suits hikers wanting minimal weight in fair to moderate weather.

Most hikers like the Gossamer Gear The One for its quick pitch, generous room for its weight and good value. Condensation is the main complaint, as with most single-wall tents, and some report silnylon sag, leaks or wear after long use. It runs small for hikers over about six feet.

Most hikers find the Katabatic Gear Palisade 30°F Quilt warmer than its rating suggests, with good build quality and a pad attachment system that keeps drafts down. A minority, mostly cold sleepers, were chilly near freezing. A few dislike the narrow cut or the fiddly straps and sewn footbox.

Most hikers find the Katabatic Gear Alsek 22°F Quilt properly warm, often comfortable around and below freezing, with good build quality and a pad attachment that works once figured out. Cold sleepers sometimes got chilly, and a few found the strap system annoying or drafty when turning. Some found it too warm in mild weather.

Most hikers find the Katabatic Gear Flex 22°F Quilt warm and comfortable, often into the teens with layers, and well made. Drafts are the main complaint, especially for restless sleepers or when moving around near freezing. The footbox opens for warm nights, and the wide size suits side sleepers.

Most hikers find the Osprey Exos 58 very comfortable for a fairly light framed pack, with a mesh back panel that keeps sweat down and room for a bear canister. Comfort fades for some once loads climb past roughly 30 pounds. A few report fit problems, the lining wearing out over time, or squeaking.

Most hikers praise the Tarptent Double Rainbow for its roomy interior, quick pitch and solid performance in wind and rain, with many long-term owners. Condensation is the main complaint, and the optional liner helps. It is tight for two and some find it heavy for what it is.

Most hikers like the MSR PocketRocket Deluxe as a small, fast-boiling stove that simmers well and copes with wind better than ultralight canister stoves. The main complaint is durability, with the piezo igniter failing early for several owners and some reports of loose parts. Many carry a backup lighter.

Most hikers find the Osprey Exos 48 comfortable for loads up to roughly 30 or 35 pounds, with excellent back airflow and a durable build that lasts years. Downsides are small, awkward hip pockets and compression strap routing, and a few found it creaky. It is not a heavy-load hauler.

Most hikers love the Big Agnes Copper Spur HV UL2 for its roomy, freestanding design, good ventilation and decent weight for the space, with many using it for years. Downsides are zippers that fail, a few reports of leaking or wearing out, and a tight fit for two with wide pads.

Most hikers find the Gossamer Gear Kumo 36 surprisingly comfortable for a frameless pack, handling around 20 to 25 pounds well, with useful pockets and a fair price. A frameless pack still tires some on long days or heavier loads. A couple report the stretchy pockets or bottom tearing, and some miss load lifters.

Most hikers find the NEMO Switchback a comfortable foam pad with no leak risk, warm enough into the 20s, and softer than similar folding pads. Downsides are bulk, firmness that some find sore as side sleepers, and the foam compressing with use. Many also use it under an inflatable for extra warmth.

Hikers praise the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite NXT for its warmth for the weight, and many find it comfortable. Comfort is divided though: some find it narrow, unstable or too slippery as side sleepers, and a few hear crinkle noise. Several report leaks, valve trouble or early failures.

Most hikers find the Durston Wapta 30 comfortable and light for a frameless pack, with tough fabric, handy pockets and a removable hip belt. Comfort holds with light kits, but the shoulder straps hurt some people, especially as loads rise. It also has to be packed carefully.

Most hikers love the Durston X-Dome 2 for its roomy interior, easy freestanding pitch and good weather handling. The main downside is durability, with several reports of bent or broken poles in strong gusts and torn floors. Some find it too big and heavy for solo use.

Most hikers like the Durston X-Mid 1 Solid for its warmth, wind and rain protection and good space for the weight, especially in cool, windy conditions. It takes practice to pitch well and can sag on uneven ground. The solid inner is stuffy in heat and humidity, and tall hikers or dog owners find it tight.

Most hikers find the Zpacks Arc Blast very comfortable and light for loads around 25 to 30 pounds, with many logging thousands of miles. Durability is split, though: several report tearing mesh, ripped belts or broken stays, especially when overloaded. A few find the frame bar or arc uncomfortable.

Most hikers find the Western Mountaineering AlpinLite reliably warm, with an accurate rating, a good draft collar and a generous cut that suits side sleepers and layering. It is heavy compared with quilts, and the roomy cut can be too big for smaller or narrower sleepers. Many owners report it lasting over a decade.

Most hikers love the ULA CDT, calling it comfortable and long-lasting, with several reporting many years of use. Being frameless, it gets uncomfortable with heavy loads such as lots of desert water, and the high side pockets and thin shoulder straps bother a few. It suits lighter solo trips.

Most hikers like the Zpacks Hexamid Pocket Tarp for its very low weight and say it handles wind and storms well when pitched carefully. Space inside is limited, especially pitched low, and it is less enclosed than a tent, so many pair it with a bivy. Very tall hikers may find their feet stick out.

Most hikers find the MSR PocketRocket 2 tough and reliable, with good simmer control, compact packing and years of trouble-free use. The main downsides are weak performance in wind and cold, and slow boils compared with pricier stoves. It suits three-season cooking.

Hikers mostly like the Toaks Titanium 750ml Pot for how much it holds inside: a small stove and canister usually nest in it, which makes a compact, light cook kit. A few note it is narrow and titanium heats unevenly, so food can burn and boils are slower than in a wider pot.

Most hikers find the Western Mountaineering SummerLite light, small and durable, and a good three-season bag. Several say it is comfortable to around freezing or a bit warmer, and that it feels like a 40F bag in practice, so cold sleepers or shoulder seasons may want more warmth. The cut is slim for broader people.

Most hikers say the Zpacks Solplex is light, quick to pitch and very durable, with many describing years of storms and long hikes without damage. Downsides are condensation, a snug interior and the need for a careful pitch in bad weather. Repairs are easy, and it suits solo hikers.

Most hikers find the Big Agnes Fly Creek UL2 light and long-lasting, with several using theirs for around a decade. It is tight inside, especially for taller people or two sleepers, and has limited headroom and vestibule space. Wind performance drew one bad report. It works best for solo use.

Most hikers like the Osprey Exos Pro 55 for its light weight, adjustable torso, ventilation and tough fabric, and several carried it on long trails. Complaints are mixed: the hip pockets lose items, some find it less comfortable than other packs, and one pack failed early. Fit takes some adjusting.

Most hikers praise the Tarptent Moment for its quick setup, small footprint and strong performance in wind and storms, with several using theirs for years. It is on the snug side for taller people, and rain on hard ground can splash silt onto it. The pole sleeve can be damaged if handled roughly.

Hikers consistently love the Western Mountaineering MegaLite for its warmth, roomy wider cut and long life, with one still using theirs after many years. Many say its ratings are conservative or on the cautious side, though one treats it as comfortable only to around freezing. It suits three-season use and side sleepers.

Most hikers love the Feathered Friends Egret UL for its warmth, comfort and fit, especially smaller and cold sleepers, and it packs very small. Sizing matters, and a bag that fits properly makes a difference. One hiker had zipper problems on a new bag.

Hikers mostly like the Hyperlite Mountain Gear UltaMid 4 for its roominess, with several fitting groups, dogs or tall users, and for its four-season weather protection and long life. A few say it is tight with big dogs and the center pole is in the way. One feels build quality has slipped.

Most hikers like the Western Mountaineering NanoLite Top Quilt as a light, well-made summer quilt whose temperature rating holds up when wearing clothes. The sewn footbox and snug straps limit its range and some find it fairly narrow in use. A couple think it is pricey versus other quilts.

Most hikers like the Zpacks Duplex Lite Tent for its very low weight, easy pitch and generous room, with one reporting a floor intact after a month of nightly use. Complaints are some condensation, sloped walls that touch taller sleepers, and doors that are awkward in rain. A few preferred an X-Mid.

Most hikers rate the Mountain Laurel Designs TrailStar highly for wind and storm performance, roomy living space and low weight for the size, with one living in it for months on the AT. The big footprint needs a large flat pitch, and the pitch has a learning curve. It is floorless and open, and a few found the corners tore.

Most hikers find the Osprey Exos 38 comfortable and roomier than its size suggests, handling two- to five-day trips and a bear canister. The main downside is capacity for longer trips and thru-hikes, where several moved to bigger packs. The outer pocket may rip, and one found it dug into the hips.

Hikers mostly like the Six Moon Designs Deschutes Plus for its light weight, quick setup and decent storm performance, with several using it on long trails and calling it a favorite. Space is tight for taller hikers, it can get steamy, and a few mention zipper or quality quirks. It suits drier trips and solo use.

Most hikers love the Zpacks Plex Solo Lite Tent for being very light, small to pack and easy to pitch, with several describing floors that look new after many nights. Space is the main drawback: taller hikers find it snug or cramped. It suits solo hikers who put weight first.

Hikers like the Gossamer Gear LT5 Three Piece Carbon Trekking Poles for their light weight, grip and solid lock feel, and they work well as tarp poles. Durability is the main worry: twist locks slipped for one, a pole broke for another, and a heavy user went through several top sections. Opinions are mixed.

Most hikers like the Jetboil Stash Cooking System as a light, fuel-efficient set that packs into one compact pot and boils quickly. Downsides are a plastic lid that deforms, a stock burner some think is average, and limited canister fit. It suits those who value fuel efficiency over the very lightest setup.

Hikers consistently like the Mountain Laurel Designs Cricket for its roomy feel, small pack size and reliable storm performance, and it can be pitched high or low. It is an open tarp, so many pair it with a bivy, and single-pole entry takes some getting used to. No clear complaints came up.

Most hikers find Gossamer Gear The Two light and fairly easy to pitch once they have practiced, and several say it handled storms well. Condensation is the main complaint, especially with two people or in cold, wet weather. A few find it tight for two or short for taller hikers, and some use a footprint under the thin floor.

Most hikers find the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Junction comfortable even with heavy loads and roomier than its listed size suggests. Downsides are scattered: a few say it makes the back sweat or has too little shoulder or hip padding, and a few report water getting in during downpours or through the bottom. It suits people wanting one roomy all-rounder.

Most hiker couples find the Enlightened Equipment Accomplice warm, spacious and comfortable, and many say the pad straps stop blanket stealing. Many pair it with a double pad and some use it with kids. A few were cold even when sharing it, one disliked the center flap, and one finds venting harder than with two quilts.

Most hikers like the versatility of the Enlightened Equipment Convert, which works as a quilt or zips up like a bag, and many find it warm and well made. The main downside is that a few, mostly cold sleepers, were cold at or near their rated temperature. It suits people wanting one flexible warm layer.

Most hikers say the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Windrider holds up well, with several reporting long thru-hikes and years of use without problems, and many find it comfortable. Complaints are scattered: the mesh pocket can snag, a few get a sweaty back, and a couple report water getting in or side bottles being hard to reach.

Most hikers find the Katabatic Gear Flex 15°F Quilt warm for its rating, comfortable well below freezing and too hot only in mild weather. The main downside is that a few cold sleepers were cold, and a couple blamed drafts from the open back. Several recommend choosing wide or long for room.

Most hikers find the Tarptent Rainbow easy to pitch, stable in storms and roomy for tall people. Condensation is the main complaint, though some say a taut pitch keeps it minor. It is not freestanding and is tight for two, and one sold it because the strut made packing a pain.

Most hikers find the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XTherm NXT very warm for its weight, including on snow and in winter, and durable over long trips. The main downside is comfort: several side sleepers got hip pressure or rolled off the narrow regular size, and one had back pain. It suits cold-weather use.

Hikers are split on the Zpacks Arc Haul. Many like its ventilation and light weight and carry it comfortably on long hikes, but the main complaint is broken stays and frame parts, including on several thru-hikes. Several find it best at about 25 lb or less, and experiences with replacements vary.

Most hikers find the Big Agnes Zoom UL Insulated very comfortable, especially for side sleeping. Many say it feels colder than expected in cool weather, several report slow leaks, and the valve and pump sack draw repeated criticism for being slow to deflate or ineffective. Some also mention crinkly noise.

Most hikers, especially side sleepers, call the Sea to Summit Ether Light XR very comfortable, and it packs small. Downsides are that a few found it colder than its rating on chilly nights, some find it noisy, and it is a bit heavier than rivals.

Most hikers love the space of the Zpacks Triplex Classic Tent for two people, often with a child or dog, at a light weight. Downsides are minor and spread out: it packs larger than expected, needs a big pitch area, is not freestanding, and a few note vestibule splashback or some single-wall condensation.

Most hikers call the Tarptent StratoSpire 2 Li very storm worthy and wind resistant, with large vestibules and plenty of room. Downsides are a pitching learning curve, struts that make packing awkward, and a narrow floor that does not take two wide pads. The double wall is credited with keeping condensation in check.

Hikers consistently call the Western Mountaineering AstraLite Top Quilt warm for its weight and well made, and many use it comfortably into the 20s °F. Minor points: the cut is a bit narrow and can be drafty at the shoulders without the straps, sizing runs confusing, and the first version had fabric problems that WM later addressed.

Most hikers find the Western Mountaineering TerraLite roomy and warm, and especially good for side sleepers who toss and turn. Several describe it as very well made and long lasting. It is on the heavy side, some find it too warm for summer, and one returned a 25 that felt cold in the 30s.

Most hikers find the Granite Gear Blaze 60 comfortable and adjustable, and it handles heavy loads well. Complaints are few: a couple had the hip belt slip or bend under load, one found its durability disappointing, and another heard a squeak. It suits heavy loads, with lighter options better for light ones.

Hikers are mixed on the Zpacks Altaplex Classic Tent. Many report it holds up well over many nights and miles and is light, while the main complaint is condensation, often leaving a damp quilt footbox. A few find the pitch finicky or the space cramped, though some tall hikers like the headroom.

Most hikers find the NEMO Hornet OSMO roomy for its weight, quick to set up, and dry in rain, with the 2P and 3P praised for two people. The 1P gets called tiny with a small vestibule. A few worry about how delicate it feels, and one returned theirs after poles and cables snapped.

Most hikers love how light the Black Diamond Distance Carbon Z Poles are, and many have used them for years, including on thru-hikes and for running. The main downside is breakage, with several snapping tips or sections, though Black Diamond often replaced them. They are fixed length, and the strap may not fit winter gloves.

Most hikers use the NEMO Tensor Extreme Conditions in cold weather or on snow and find it warm and comfortable, including for side sleeping. Complaints are rare and scattered: one found warmth its drawback, and one reported a pad failure within days.

Most hikers like the Six Moon Designs Skyscape Trekker, especially tall hikers who find it roomy and long enough, and several praise its light weight, easy setup and ventilation with doors that roll back. The main complaint is condensation, including feet touching the roof, and a couple dislike the detailing.
Hikers say the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Mid 1 is quick and easy to pitch. It fits tall users, but some at about 6'2" or more find it a close fit, with the wall near their face.
Hikers mostly love the Six Moon Designs Swift X, especially the comfort of its vest-style straps, and say it holds plenty. A couple could not get comfortable in it and returned or swapped it.
Hikers find the Tarptent Rainbow Li roomy and light, with tall hikers fitting comfortably. Condensation can build in cold weather, but several find it minor or manageable, especially with the liner.
Hikers describe the Tarptent Double Rainbow DW as sturdy and easy to pitch, though a few find a perfectly taut pitch hard to get.
Hikers who accept the extra weight like the Big Agnes Copper Spur UL1 for its easy freestanding pitch and generous storage. Room is mostly praised, though one finds it cramped for a quilt.
Hikers find the Feathered Friends Flicker UL Quilt warm and long-lasting, with some using it for years and several sleeping comfortably in it on cold nights.
Hikers with years of Hornet use call the NEMO Hornet Elite OSMO light, durable and storm-worthy, and several name the OSMO versions their favorite so far.
Hikers say the Jetboil MiniMo Cooking System boils fast and has good simmer control, so it works for real cooking as well as boiling water.
Hikers find the Osprey Eja 48 comfortable on long hikes, including full thru-hikes, but it gets very tight once a bear can goes in. Some add their own hip pockets.

Hikers find the Hyperlite Mountain Gear 20-Degree Quilt warm, with several sleeping comfortably near freezing and below, and roomy enough for side and restless sleepers. A couple call it pricey at full price.
Hikers like the Hyperlite Mountain Gear UltaMid 2 as a strong shelter that handles all seasons and storms, and it works for two. Some note it is heavy and pricey.
Hikers find the Tarptent StratoSpire 2 very roomy, fitting couples with a dog or even a family with a sidecar, and several have used it for years.

Hikers like the ULA Ohm for comfortable suspension that carries weight well, and for its big pockets. A few hit quirks, such as a stiff hip belt that did not suit one hiker's shape or the pack bulging widthwise.
Hikers who like the Zpacks Pivot Solo Tent praise its small footprint and handling of rain, but several find it fussy to pitch taut and say storm performance depends on the pitch.
Hikers who love the Mountain Laurel Designs SoloMid XL call it their go-to solo shelter, but a few tall hikers find it a tight fit with the wall close to their face.
Hikers mostly call the Big Agnes Copper Spur UL2 roomy, including for tall hikers and for one person. Some report moisture trouble, from condensation to a floor that wet out in rain.
Hikers like the Big Agnes Tiger Wall UL1 as a light, easy-to-pitch solo tent that holds up to hard use and wind. It suits smaller hikers best.

Hikers like the Enlightened Equipment Conundrum for its roomy, bag-like cut with a footbox and good warmth in deep cold. A couple were cold, one at the shoulders when clipped to a pad and one well above its rating.
Hikers like the Sea to Summit Spark for packing very small, but many find it colder than expected, needing a liner or extra layers even above the rating.
Hikers like the Sea to Summit Spark Pro for its open footbox and zips that let them vent on mild nights, and several slept warm when it turned cold. Some find it roomy.
Hikers love the Osprey Eja 58 for comfort on long days and for how well it cinches down when not full.
Hikers rate the Katabatic Gear Flex 40°F Quilt highly, and a couple stayed warm in it down to about freezing.
Hikers find the Zpacks Duplex Classic Tent easy to pitch in minutes and solid in wind and rain, roomy for one person and workable for two.
Hikers like the Granite Gear Crown3 60 as a comfortable, budget-friendly pack that carried them through thru-hikes, with a removable lid to save weight.
